title: Parks Canada budget cuts, tourism growth raise concerns for Canada Strong Pass return
summary: The return of the Canada Strong Pass is getting mixed reviews. The pass will come back for a third year as Parks Canada is intending to lay off 517 full-time positions, and Banff National Park hit a…

image.caption: Banff has seen increased visitation in recent years with or without the Canada Strong Pass, which is set to return for a third year in 2027. (John Gibson/CBC)

blocks.text: Calgary·New

The return of the Canada Strong Pass is getting mixed reviews. The pass will come back for a third year as Parks Canada is intending to lay off 517 full-time positions, and Banff National Park hit a record 4.5 million visitors.
'Free admission should not come with fewer services,' says union
The return of the Canada Strong Pass is getting mixed reviews.

The pass will come back for a third year as Parks Canada is intending to lay off 517 full-time positions, and Banff National Park hit a record 4.5 million visitors. It provides free admission to Parks Canada sites over the summer.

“I think it’s really commendable, but it needs to have better strategy to go along with it, and currently we’re lacking the strategic part of implementing this really well meaning initiative,” said Banff Mayor Corrie DiManno.

She said the municipality has pushed to have the pass in off-peak seasons such as October and November or March and April. She said other ideas are free entry after 5 p.m., promoting public transit and carpooling, and only giving Canadians free entry.

items: Lake Louise, Moraine need new approach to tourism, says Parks Canada. What that looks like is still unclear

blocks.text: The specific dates haven’t been announced, but the federal budget stated the pass would return this summer.

Parks Canada is receiving $76 million for estimated lost revenue from free entry and discounted camping. The federal agency received about $160 million for the previous two summers and one winter the Canada Strong Pass ran.
DiManno said its return was “quite the surprise and shock” since Parks Canada is expected to reduce its resources in early 2027.
“We’re definitely concerned these budget reductions could have an impact on services that visitors and residents really rely on,” she said.
Parks Canada cuts coming in 2027

Jean-Michel Lavergne, the president of the Union of National Employees, which represents most Parks Canada staff, said it’s important for people to visit national parks. But he said increasing visitations while removing staff is a contradiction.

“If free admission brings more visitors, it means more maintenance, more demands for information and greater pressure on facilities,” he said. “Our members on the ground are really worried how they’ll be able to offer the same services with less people.”
As directed by Prime Minister Mark Carney, 10 to 15 per cent of savings from federal ministries, agencies and departments are expected in the next three years.

blocks.text: For Parks Canada, that means about $145 million in cuts.
The federal agency sent out 2,917 letters to employees — more than half of Parks Canada workers — that their jobs could be cut or their roles changed.

Lavergne said the union has been meeting with Parks Canada biweekly, but there remain unknowns. Parks Canada staff have until Nov. 23 to take a voluntary retirement or buyout. Lavergne said the union requested an extra 30 days to allow staff to get more information on the changes, which Parks Canada denied.
He said Parks Canada staff take pride in welcoming visitors, but “free admission should not come with fewer services.”
“Our members want to welcome more visitors, but they need the resources to do it properly.”
Banff townsite consistently busy in summer
According to statistics from the Town of Banff, 1.77 million vehicles entered the townsite in July and August — an all-time high.
In 2022, the last year personal vehicles could travel to Moraine Lake, there were an estimated 700,000 visitors.
With more than 200 commercial vehicle operators, Parks Canada estimates visitation now hits about one million people a year.
Lake Louise also remains busy. Parks Canada estimates about 3,300 people visit daily in personal vehicles and about 2,700 on buses.
Roughly half of the visitors on buses are Canadians, according to Parks Canada.

In a statement from the Department of Canadian Heritage, spokesperson Martine Courage said the pass’s return is meant “to make it easier and more affordable for Canadians to explore this country and enjoy its cultural, historical and natural treasures.”
She said it also coincides with Canada’s 160th anniversary.
Courage said the summer was picked since “most children and youth are out of school and have more time to visit cultural institutions and attractions or travel domestically.”
The pass also provides youth with free or discounted access to national museums and galleries, and VIA Rail tickets.
A spokesperson from Parks Canada's national communications team didn't get back to CBC News before publishing.
Banff National Park turns 140 years old

DiManno isn't convinced the increased traffic to Banff is thanks to the Canada Strong Pass — she said summer is peak season no matter what. She noted Calgary and the surrounding area are growing, and increased costs for gas and flights are driving Canadians to travel closer to home.
“It would be great if it can be implemented differently here in Banff,” she said.
